episodes.title: Lynching of John Riggins
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Riggins took place near Bainbridge, Decatur County, Georgia, on the evening of August 17, 1915, when searching parties shot to death a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman. After the woman identified him, his captors killed him with about 100 shots. The killing happened the same day as the lynching of Leo Frank, and a Black correspondent in the Savannah Tribune pointed to the contrast between the two cases.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Boney and Willie Kirksey
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Ben Boney and Willie Kirksey took place at Meridian, Mississippi, in August 1915, after the two Black men were arrested on the accusation of stopping a woman's buggy on the Causeyville road. With a crowd gathered and a lynching feared, the sheriff sent them out of the county under guard. Mississippi papers later reported that the two had been indicted and then found innocent, and carried the story as "Nearly Lynched Wrong Men."

episodes.title: Lynching of Will Leach
episodes.summary: The lynching of Will Leach took place on the night of August 5-6, 1915, when a mob took Leach, a Black man, from the jail at Dade City, Florida, and hanged him at Trilby. Leach was charged with attacking a thirteen-year-old white girl at Trilby, and his killing was reported nationally by the Associated Press and in a Memphis roundup of nine Black men hanged in the South in a single day.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sam Jernagan
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Sam Jernagan was a failed attempt by a mob in Trinity County, Texas, in the summer of 1915 to lynch a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white girl. Sheriff Thornton moved Jernagan to the jail at Houston, and in August state troops guarded him at his trial in Groveton, where he was convicted and sentenced to death. Texas editorials held up the sheriff's refusal to yield to the mob as an example for other officers.

episodes.title: Lynching of King and Joe Richmond
episodes.summary: The lynching of King and Joe Richmond took place on August 29, 1915, in Sulphur Springs, Texas, when a crowd burned King Richmond, a wounded Black man, at the stake in Buford Park together with the body of his brother Joe, whom a posse had killed hours earlier. The brothers had been accused of killing Deputy Sheriff Nathan A. Flippen and wounding Sheriff J. B. Butler of Hopkins County that morning. Wire reports of a crowd of thousands and a burning moved from the town square to a park ran nationally, and several Black weeklies answered with editorials.

episodes.title: Lynching near Coushatta, Louisiana (1915)
episodes.summary: The lynching near Coushatta, Louisiana, was the hanging of an unidentified Black man by a mob of armed men early on Saturday, August 21, 1915, after he was accused of entering the bedroom of a farmer's 17-year-old daughter and trying to assault her. The mob took the man from a deputy sheriff who had him in custody and hanged him in a nearby swamp. The killing was reported in brief wire items in white newspapers from Alabama to Idaho over the following week.

episodes.title: Exclusion of Black people from Forsyth County, Georgia (1915)
episodes.summary: The exclusion of Black people from Forsyth County, Georgia, was reported in late August 1915, when an Atlanta dispatch stated that all Black people had been barred from entering the county after trouble between whites and blacks there and in neighboring territory. The dispatch illustrated the ban with an incident at Cumming, where a crowd of several hundred threatened two Black servants of an Atlanta visitor with violence unless they left the county at once. The story ran in white papers from Virginia to Missouri and was reprinted in Black weeklies into mid-September.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Collins
episodes.summary: The lynching of Thomas Collins was the hanging by a mob of a Black man at Bunkie, Louisiana, first reported on August 1, 1915. Collins was accused of shooting and wounding a policeman who had tried to arrest him. A special grand jury called to investigate the lynching reported that it could not find enough evidence to hold anyone responsible.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ernest Chappell
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Ernest Chappell took place at Fitzpatrick, in Twiggs County, Georgia, around August 1, 1915, when a mob formed to take Chappell, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and lynch him. Sheriff Wimberly moved Chappell and the jail's only other inmate, Will Thomas, to the Bibb County jail in Macon before the mob acted. The episode reached the press as a short Macon dispatch printed in Georgia and South Carolina.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Gent Jenkins
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Gent Jenkins was a proposed mob action in Muskogee, Oklahoma, in August 1915 against a Black man arrested after the hatchet murder of white grocer Wm. B. Province. According to the Muskogee Cimeter, a Black weekly, the forming mob dissolved after police and the sheriff warned it would meet deadly force, and Jenkins was discharged. Weeks later the victim's widow was charged with the murder.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Smith
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Robert Smith occurred in Talbot County, Maryland, in late August 1915, when residents around Royal Oak uttered threats against Smith, a Black youth jailed at Easton on a charge of assaulting a young white girl. Talk of lynching subsided after State's Attorney Charles J. Butler had a special grand jury called, and Smith was indicted, granted a change of venue, and tried at Elkton in September. Papers in four states and Alexandria carried the case, several pairing it with the hanging of "Wish" Sheppard at Denton that week.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bob Baker and King Lyons
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Bob Baker and King Lyons was a mob's failed attempt in August 1915 to take two Black men accused of murdering a white sawmill owner from the Concordia parish jail at Vidalia, Louisiana. Sheriff Eugene Campbell refused a decoy call meant to draw him away and rowed the prisoners across the Mississippi River to Natchez before the mob could reach them. Mississippi papers reported the episode as a mob foiled by the sheriff.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Fox
episodes.summary: The lynching of James Fox took place in August 1915 at the camp of the Alger-Sullivan Lumber Company, eight miles north of Tunnel Springs, Alabama, where a mob pursued, shot and hanged a Black man accused of wounding a deputy sheriff. The only account came from a special dispatch to the Mobile Item, which was reprinted in Alabama, Tennessee and South Carolina and condensed into one-line items in Wisconsin and Kentucky weeklies.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Kid Henderson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Kid Henderson occurred at Chandler, Oklahoma, in early August 1915, when Henderson, a Black man accused of a killing at nearby Wellston, was rushed to the state penitentiary to keep him from a lynching. Henderson pleaded guilty and was sentenced to prison, and no mob attack was reported.

episodes.title: Lynching threat against Charles Davis
episodes.summary: The lynching threat against Charles Davis took place at Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in August 1915, when talk of lynching Davis, a Black man held in the county jail on horse-stealing charges, led Sheriff Hardy to post an armed guard. No attack on the jail was reported, and the guard was withdrawn the next day.

episodes.title: Mock lynching of two Black prisoners at Williston, Florida
episodes.summary: The mock lynching of two Black prisoners at Williston, Florida, took place in Levy County in or before August 1915, when two Black men held on a charge of cow stealing were roped by the neck, hoisted and choked to force them to confess. A local paper, the Williston Courier, first reported that the county sheriff had been seen in the woods trying to lynch the men, but the Ocala Evening Star later called that story a fake and reported that the sheriff blamed men of Williston. The case drew notice in the Florida press chiefly as a dispute over the sheriff's conduct.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry McNeal
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Henry McNeal took place in Lawton, Oklahoma, on 21 August 1915, when a mob began forming to take McNeal, a 30-year-old Black man accused of attempting to assault a white woman. He was moved from the city jail to the guard house at Fort Sill, and no one was killed. An Oklahoma paper described the episode as a narrowly averted "race war," and the Indianapolis Freeman reported that Black residents, many of them women dressed as men, had driven the mob off.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fat Ward
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Fat Ward took place at Greer, South Carolina, on the night of Sunday, August 15, 1915, when a mob gathered outside the town lockup where Ward, a Black man, was held after a shooting during his arrest. A doctor and a town officer drove him to the Spartanburg jail before the crowd acted.

episodes.title: Lynching of Kit Jackson and Harry Russell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Kit Jackson and Harry Russell was the shooting of three Black men by four white men near Hope Hull, at McGehee's Switch in Montgomery County, Alabama, early on August 18, 1915; Jackson and Harry Russell were killed and Ed Russell was left for dead. The three were free on bond on an untried charge of poisoning livestock. Wire reports carried it nationally as the lynching of three men, and Black weeklies cited it as a case that drew little notice beside the lynching of Leo Frank the day before.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Deberry
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Joe Deberry was a series of mob attempts in southern Illinois between July 30 and August 30, 1915, to seize and hang Deberry, a Black servant accused of murdering Mrs. James H. Martin, a Murphysboro lawyer's wife. Officers kept him from mobs at Murphysboro, Marion and Harrisburg, and militia guarded his trial, where he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to hang. Southern papers cited the case to answer the Chicago Tribune's criticism of lynching in the South.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Berry
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ed Berry was the hanging of a Black man by masked men in Shawnee, Oklahoma, early on August 6, 1915, after he was taken from a deputy sheriff who was bringing him to trial. Berry was charged with criminal assaults on white women, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of a mob of persons unknown. A Shawnee dispatch calling it "one of the most orderly lynchings in the history of the state" was repeated in white and Black papers across the country.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sam Johnson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Sam Johnson occurred in Colusa and Yolo counties, California, in August 1915, when posses and crowds of ranchers threatened to lynch Johnson, a Black man accused of fatally shooting Richard Lindsay and attacking Lindsay's aunt, Mrs. Michael Blevins. A member of the searching party fired four shots at Johnson before his capture near Capay on August 3, and a crowd gathered at the Woodland depot to meet his train. The Colusa County sheriff evaded a mob by driving Johnson to the jail at Marysville, and a month later the accused, there named "Sam Robertson," was reported to have pleaded guilty and been sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Forced levee labor at Newport, Arkansas (1915)
episodes.summary: The forced levee labor at Newport, Arkansas, was the reported compulsion of Black men, at the point of shotguns, to work on the town's flooding levees on the night of August 22-23 and the morning of August 23, 1915. According to one wire version, armed white citizens threatened the workers with death if they relaxed. No one was reported hurt, and the claim reached papers from Arizona to Wisconsin as a line in flood news.

episodes.title: 1915 Clay County manhunt
episodes.summary: The 1915 Clay County manhunt was a search by a posse of up to 500 armed men, with bloodhounds, for an unnamed Black man accused of attacking Mrs. Henry Stafford in her farm home near Liberty, Clay County, Missouri, on August 5, 1915. Papers reported talk of lynching and predicted the man would be killed if caught, but the hounds lost the trail, rain ended the search on August 7, and no capture was reported. The hunt went out over the wires and was folded into roundups of a day of hangings and lynchings in the South, which the Chicago Defender reprinted under the headline "Nine Human Beings Hanged in South Within 24 Hours."

episodes.title: Dynamiting of a Black church in Wellston, Oklahoma
episodes.summary: The dynamiting of a Black church in Wellston, Oklahoma, took place on a Saturday night in early August 1915, when unknown persons exploded a stick of dynamite under the town's "negro church." The blast damaged the building but injured no one, and no clue to the dynamiter was found. Oklahoma papers reported it as an "echo" of the mob lynching of Ed Berry at Shawnee the day before.

episodes.title: Wynn "possum hunter" whippings
episodes.summary: The Wynn "possum hunter" whippings were a night raid in mid-August 1915 in which fifteen masked, armed men went to the homes of white and Black residents near Wynn, in northern Christian County, Kentucky, whipped several people, and left notices ordering them out of the community. One white man and one Black woman were known to have been whipped, and two white men who had been warned left the area. Papers outside Kentucky ran the story as a revival of night riding in western Kentucky, and one dispatch warned of a "race war."

episodes.title: Hastings Street riot (Detroit, 1915)
episodes.summary: The Hastings Street riot was a street fight in Detroit, Michigan, on the evening of Sunday, August 1, 1915, between Jewish and Black residents of the Hastings Street neighborhood, set off when a crowd chased and besieged a Black man accused of snatching a woman's handbag. Two men of the crowd were stabbed, another man was shot in the foot and a woman was stabbed, and police arrested five Black men; no one was reported killed. Wire services carried it as a 'race riot' between Jews and Negroes, and one Black weekly reprinted it under the headline "Negroes Check Mob."

episodes.title: "Possum Hunters" warning to J. K. McGoodwin, Princeton, Kentucky
episodes.summary: The "Possum Hunters" warning to J. K. McGoodwin was a written threat left in August 1915 at the brickyard of McGoodwin, a brick manufacturer in Princeton, Kentucky, ordering him to get rid of his Black laborers or lose his life. McGoodwin dismissed his Black workers at once. Newspapers outside Kentucky noted the case chiefly because McGoodwin was described as the father of the United States minister to Venezuela, and they reported it as part of a wave of night riding in Caldwell and Christian counties.

episodes.title: Police killing of a Black man at City Point, Virginia (1915)
episodes.summary: The police killing of a Black man at City Point, Virginia, took place on the night of August 8, 1915, when a police officer shot dead an unnamed Black man he was trying to arrest. According to the only report, the man resisted arrest and fired at the officer, and an inquest exonerated the officer.

episodes.title: Killing of Jacob Brooks
episodes.summary: The killing of Jacob Brooks was the fatal shooting of Brooks, a Black man, by Henry Allen, a special officer at a fertilizer plant, in Alexandria, Virginia, on August 22, 1915. A coroner's jury exonerated Allen the next day, finding that he had fired in self-defense after Brooks, whom he had under arrest, seized his club and attacked him. The Alexandria Gazette counted Brooks as the sixth Black man shot dead by city officers; the only Black-press notice was a brief in the Denver Star weeks later.

episodes.title: Execution of Robert Watkins and John Salter
episodes.summary: The execution of Robert Watkins and John Salter was the legal hanging of two Black men at Evergreen, Alabama, on August 6, 1915, for the murder of a white woman, Mrs. Mary Lassiter. Militia stood guard at the gallows, and wire reports said a crowd of citizens had demanded that the two men be burned. The case reached the national press as one of nine hangings of Black men in the South in a single day, a roundup the Chicago Defender reprinted under the headline "Nine Human Beings Hanged in South Within 24 Hours."

episodes.title: Exclusion of Black laborers from the Oklahoma State Capitol construction
episodes.summary: The exclusion of Black laborers from the Oklahoma State Capitol construction took place in Oklahoma City in August 1915, when white building-trades workers objected to Black men employed as common laborers on the new Capitol. The contractor agreed that only white union labor would do the unskilled work, and the Black laborers were let go. The Tulsa Star, a Black weekly, treated the episode as an affront to Black taxpayers who were helping pay for the building.

episodes.title: Killing of Abram Hardy
episodes.summary: The killing of Abram Hardy took place on August 30, 1915, in Newberry County, South Carolina, when three officers shot Hardy, a Black man of about 40, while trying to arrest him near his home. A coroner's jury found that day that they had acted in the discharge of their duties, and they were released on bail. The Newberry Herald and News printed the inquest testimony in full under the headline "Preferred Death to Being Arrested."

episodes.title: Greenville shooting of Huston Herbert
episodes.summary: The Greenville shooting of Huston Herbert was an exchange of gunfire on the night of August 11, 1915, in Greenville, Alabama, between Huston Herbert, a Black man, and a party of county and city officers who had come to his home in search of his brother. About twenty-three revolver shots were fired, but no one was reported hit, and neither Herbert brother had been taken by the following evening.

episodes.title: Killing of Walter Tucker
episodes.summary: The killing of Walter Tucker was the fatal shooting of a 27-year-old Black man by Marshal James Walker of Brownsville, apparently in Tennessee, on August 23, 1915. Walker shot Tucker while trying to arrest him, and the only report found gives the officer's account that Tucker resisted.

episodes.title: Shooting of Ode Johnson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Ode Johnson took place in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in mid-August 1915, when Captain George F. Lumb, assistant superintendent of the State Police, fired on Johnson, a Black man, and wounded him in the right leg as he fled from an alleged attempted assault on a woman near Lumb's home. Johnson was arrested, failed to win release on a writ of habeas corpus, and was convicted at the September quarter sessions and sentenced to six months. The Harrisburg Telegraph, the only paper found to cover the case, followed it from a weekend crime roundup through the court columns.

episodes.title: Killing of Ed Walls
episodes.summary: The killing of Ed Walls was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a police officer, A. L. Brookins, at 111 South Thirty-ninth street, apparently in Birmingham, Alabama, at about 1:40 a.m. on August 16, 1915. Walls had just been arrested on a woman's complaint, and the only report, in the Birmingham Age-Herald, gave the officers' account that he seized a pistol and fired before he was shot.

episodes.title: Peonage case of Frank Hatten
episodes.doubt: date is the Dothan arraignment (Aug 18); the whipping and holding are undated
episodes.summary: The peonage case of Frank Hatten was a federal prosecution in Alabama in August 1915, in which Rhett Flemming, a Coffee County farmer, was charged with holding Hatten, a Black laborer, in peonage. On August 18 Flemming was bound over to the federal grand jury at Dothan after Hatten testified that he had been brought back to work each time he left and had once been whipped for about two hours with a leather strap.

episodes.title: Killing of Irene Hawkins
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; July event reported in August
episodes.summary: The killing of Irene Hawkins took place on July 25, 1915, at the Savoy Hotel in Nashville, Tennessee, where Hawkins, a young Black chambermaid, was found dead in the alley beneath the window of a white guest's room. A coroner's jury charged the guest, E. J. Seymour, with raping and murdering her, and he was held in $2,500 bond. The case was carried only by Black weeklies, which used it to argue that crime was not confined to one race, and it prompted Black Nashville to raise money for the prosecution.
